facts.fact: The species was described by Linnaeus in 1758.
Phoxinus laevis is an older name for this species.
It is rated Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (assessed 12 January 2024).
It is described as arguably the UK's nicest native freshwater fish, particularly in breeding colours.
It ranges across Eurasia from the Garonne in France east to the Anadyr and Amur drainages and Korea.
It occurs in Atlantic, North Sea, Baltic, Arctic and northern Pacific basins, reaching 58°N in Great Britain.
It may have been introduced to Ireland.
It is native to the UK.
It lives in cold, well-oxygenated water, from small fast streams to large lakes.
It is usually found with salmonid fishes.
It lives in fresh and brackish water near the bottom and migrates within rivers.
FishBase lists it as commercial in the aquarium trade. It is also a minor commercial fishery fish and is often used as bait.
It is a robust species but sensitive to warm water, so it must be kept cool.
The Rainbow minnow (Notropis chrosomus) and Gold minnow (Pimephales promelas 'Gold') are often sold under similar names. They are different species.
It needs a tank of at least 200 litres, and larger is better.
In an aquarium it needs strong current and high oxygen levels.
In the wild it eats algae, plant debris, molluscs, crustaceans and insects.
It is omnivorous and prefers animal food.
In aquaria it accepts flake food. Mosquito larvae, daphnia and artemia, fresh or frozen, are recommended.
It is gregarious.
It is a peaceful, lively schooling fish that forms close shoals and swims a lot.
It is compatible with gudgeons, bitterlings and whitefish.
During spawning, males show stronger colours and develop white spawning tubercles on the head and gill covers.
Females are fuller and larger than males.
In the wild it migrates upstream to spawn over clean gravel in flowing water or on wave-washed lake shores.
It spawns in spring, scattering eggs over gravel or aquatic plants.
Aquarium breeding is possible but demanding. The parents must be removed after spawning.
